articles.headline: Fed Expected to Do Nothing Loudly, While Declining to Say What It Will Do Next
articles.dek: Chairman Kevin Warsh is expected to hold rates this week after September's hike, with forecasters split on whether he should be tightening at all.
articles.catch_up: The Fed raised rates by a quarter point in September as inflation climbed, with CPI at 3.7% and energy prices surging. Its new chairman, Kevin Warsh, has said he dislikes forward guidance, the habit of telling markets what the Fed plans next.
articles.why_it_matters: Higher rates mean mortgages above 7% and costlier car and consumer loans, while the Fed's own silence leaves borrowers and investors guessing. A mistake in either direction would land hardest on housing and household budgets.
body: The Federal Reserve is widely expected to leave interest rates unchanged when it announces its decision Wednesday, CNBC reported. Futures markets put the chance of a hike this week at about 10%, and 93% of respondents in CNBC's Fed Survey of 30 fund managers, strategists and economists also expect a pause. The central bank will thus hold a closely watched meeting in order to do nothing, which is a lot of attention for a rounding error.

The harder part is what Warsh says, or declines to say. He has pushed the Fed away from forward guidance. Translation: forward guidance means the Fed tells markets where rates are going, and Warsh would prefer that markets figure it out from the data, like everyone else with a mortgage. Deutsche Bank's Brett Ryan expects him to signal that more tightening will likely be needed over time, while skipping October buys more time to assess the data.

The data are not helping him relax. Annual CPI was 3.7% in September, driven largely by energy prices. Core CPI, which strips out gas and groceries, was 2.6%, up 0.3 percentage point from August and still above the Fed's 2% target. Translation: even the version of inflation designed to ignore the scary parts is going the wrong way.

Meanwhile the economy is sending mixed notes. Mortgage rates above 7% are squeezing housing, and CNBC described a low-fire, low-hire labor market with layoffs near their lowest since the late 1960s. Unemployment is 4.2%. Futures see better than 80% odds of a December hike, and Evercore ISI's Krishna Guha reads the Fed's baseline as roughly one hike per quarter, with the right to change its mind.

Economists disagree on whether any of this is wise. Janus Henderson's Richard Bernstein called the Fed's hesitancy to raise rates unfathomable. Moody's Mark Zandi says inflation is high but not entrenched and this is not the time for more hikes. Allianz's Mohamed El-Erian expects hikes but calls them the wrong tool, arguing for fiscal containment instead. He expects the pain to land on housing, car loans and consumer loans rather than on tech.

The survey adds a list of other worries: the war in Iran, an AI bubble, and the congressional election next week. Half of respondents blame government debt over AI borrowing for high bond yields, and the 10-year Treasury yield stands at 5.0%. Respondents expect two hikes next year on average, and a 26% chance of recession.

The likeliest outcome Wednesday is a hold, a carefully worded statement and a chairman explaining at length why he will not explain. Watch for dissents: survey respondents expect at least two voters to object to keeping rates unchanged.
articles.wire_headline: Fed expected to hold rates steady, but Warsh may point way to more hikes

articles.headline: U.S. Borrows $2 Trillion a Year, Bond Market Asks for 5.1% and a Plan
articles.dek: A $1.992 trillion deficit, a 5%-plus 10-year yield and a divided Congress on the way leave no obvious exit from the debt problem, CNBC reported.
articles.catch_up: The U.S. deficit hit $1.992 trillion in fiscal 2026, up 12% from last year, while the 10-year Treasury yield has climbed 114 basis points since the Iran war began on Feb. 28. Companies borrowing heavily for AI infrastructure are now competing with the government for the same pool of investor money.
articles.why_it_matters: The 10-year yield sets the tone for mortgage rates, which hover around 7.5%, and for what the government pays to borrow, which feeds back into the deficit. Without a political fix, higher rates make the debt harder to shrink and everyday borrowing more expensive.
body: The federal government ran a deficit of $1.992 trillion in the 2026 fiscal year, Treasury data showed Friday, according to CNBC. That is up 12% from last year and roughly 6.2% of GDP. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has said the target should be below 4% by the end of President Trump's term, which CNBC politely describes as something the U.S. has almost no way of hitting.

Meanwhile, the 10-year Treasury yield traded at 5.1% on Friday, up 114 basis points since the end of February. Translation: a basis point is one hundredth of a percentage point, so the government's borrowing cost has risen by about 1.14 percentage points in under eight months. The latest official reading, from Oct. 23, put it at 5.0%.

Several things are pushing yields up. The war with Iran sent oil and diesel prices higher, and bond traders now want extra yield in case central banks, including the Federal Reserve, raise rates. Translation: lenders are charging more now because they expect to be hurt by inflation later. Brent crude was at $115.22 as of Oct. 20, which suggests they have a point.

There is also a supply problem. Investors believe Washington will keep issuing bonds in volume, and corporations are issuing hundreds of billions in new debt to build AI infrastructure. CNBC noted that global investors seeking safe long-term debt now have attractive alternatives to Treasurys. The government, once the only borrower in the room, is now one of several people asking for the same money.

Ordinary people feel this through housing. The average 30-year mortgage hovers near 7.5%, and Redfin said pending home sales fell 4% in September, the biggest monthly drop in three years. Mortgage rates follow the 10-year yield, so a debate in Washington about spending becomes a debate in your kitchen about whether the house is still affordable.

Rates also make the deficit itself worse. The Congressional Budget Office estimates that if rates stay half a point above its forecast, the 10-year cumulative deficit will be $1.9 trillion higher, and $6 trillion higher if they overshoot by 1.5 points. The CBO expects the 10-year yield to average 4.3% over the period, against 5.1% today. In other words, the budget office is assuming rates will behave better than they currently are.

Bessent's answer is growth. "We've got this mountain of debt, and we have to grow our way out of it," he said in Dallas last month. The Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget calculates that balancing the budget by growth alone would take a decade of 7.2% GDP growth. Second-quarter growth was recently revised up from 1.5% to 2.2% annualized, so the gap is a mere five percentage points.

Politics offers little help. Republicans are widely forecast to lose at least the House in the Nov. 3 midterms, and Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, the likely next speaker, wants to reverse $1 trillion in healthcare cuts. Trump, meanwhile, pledged $5,000 checks to every adult citizen if Republicans swept the election, according to CNBC. Divided government can produce surprising compromises, though the starting positions are not close.

Not everyone sees a capital shortage. World Bank President Ajay Banga told CNBC that availability of capital is "not really an issue," noting the bank mobilized $112 billion last year, about triple the figure three years earlier. He said investors may worry about circular financing and AI business models, but emerging markets face less hesitancy because they fund bridges and roads. MarketWatch, for its part, reported that AI financing has become harder and costlier as scrutiny of the spending boom grows.

CNBC's bottom line is that a full debt crisis remains further out, and that high yields also attract buyers to Treasurys, since expensive borrowing is not the same as a crisis. Nobody knows what debt level is unsustainable, though the total reached $40 trillion this year. The one thing the bond market has not priced in is a bipartisan plan, which may be the most reasonable assumption on the board.
articles.wire_headline: Analysis: Why a $2 trillion deficit and 5% Treasury yields are becoming America's biggest economic challenge

articles.headline: Boeing Promises to Build Planes Faster Eventually, Investors Hear 'Eventually' and Sell 9%
articles.dek: Boeing says it won't significantly raise 737 Max output until late 2027 because wings are arriving slowly, even as losses narrow and defense sales climb.
articles.catch_up: Boeing has spent years trying to stabilize production of its best-selling 737 Max after a long run of safety and quality problems. On Tuesday it reported third-quarter results and updated investors on when it expects to build more planes.
articles.why_it_matters: Boeing collects most of an aircraft's price only when the customer takes delivery, so slower production means slower cash for the company and later planes for airlines. Travelers and investors should expect the recovery to be gradual rather than quick.
body: Boeing said on Tuesday that it does not expect to significantly ramp up production of the 737 Max until the second half of 2027, according to CNBC. CEO Kelly Ortberg said the target is 52 planes a month, up from about 47 now. The stated reason is a slower-than-expected pace of wing production, which is a fairly fundamental part of an airplane. Boeing shares fell about 9% during the call.

The delay is the story, though the quarter itself was less grim. Boeing reported a net loss of $116 million, or 26 cents a share, compared with a $5.34 billion loss a year earlier. Translation: the company lost far less money, mostly because last year's comparison included a nearly $5 billion charge on the long-delayed 777X program. Adjusted for one-time items, the loss was 34 cents a share, against the 21-cent loss analysts had expected, according to LSEG consensus estimates.

Revenue rose 4% to $24.19 billion, ahead of the $23.84 billion forecast. Free cash flow, the cash left after paying for operations and investment, rose to $464 million from $238 million. Boeing delivered 161 commercial airplanes, one more than a year earlier, which is technically growth and the sort of increase a company would describe as stability.

The weak spot was the commercial aircraft unit, the part of Boeing that makes the things people actually fly in. Its revenue fell 3% to $10.72 billion, and it posted a negative operating margin of 6.5%. Translation: for every dollar of sales it lost about six and a half cents on operations. Boeing blamed a less favorable delivery mix, higher projected costs tied to future production rate changes, and higher estimated supply chain costs, a list that covers most of the ways to lose money building aircraft.

Defense carried the quarter. Revenue in that unit jumped 15% to $7.94 billion, and the U.S. Navy picked Boeing to develop its next-generation fighter jet. On the civil side, the FAA approved the 737 Max 10 last week, following the Max 7 in August, which completes certification of the Max family. Boeing can now legally sell every version of the plane it is not yet building fast enough.

Ortberg struck a patient tone. 'We're going to do it right,' he told CNBC's Phil LeBeau, acknowledging that everybody wants the company to go faster. In a note to staff he said expectations are rising 'and they should,' and that the company has more work to do. Investors, who had apparently hoped for faster, responded by selling.

The logic is straightforward. Airlines are waiting on planes, Boeing is waiting on wings, and shareholders are waiting on cash, which arrives mostly at delivery. Next 52 planes a month is the number to watch, along with whether the wing supply improves before 2027 turns into 2028.
articles.wire_headline: Boeing stock sinks 9% as company says it won't significantly ramp up 737 Max production until late 2027

articles.headline: Honda Calls 50% Canada Tariff 'Catastrophic,' Hopes Cooler Heads Prevail Before New Year
articles.dek: An American Honda executive warned that doubling duties on Canadian vehicles and parts on Jan. 1 would hurt the entire industry, and asked for a three-country deal instead of two separate ones.
articles.catch_up: President Trump has threatened to raise tariffs on Canadian vehicles and parts from 25% to 50% on Jan. 1 if the U.S. and Canada fail to reach a trade deal. The U.S. has also declined to automatically extend the USMCA, the North American trade pact, putting it on an annual review.
articles.why_it_matters: Cars built in North America cross borders many times before they reach a showroom, so tariff changes can raise costs across the whole supply chain. Buyers could eventually see that in sticker prices, though the sources do not say by how much.
body: Jennifer Thomas, senior vice president of corporate affairs at American Honda Motor, told a Reuters automotive conference in Detroit on Tuesday that a 50% tariff on Canadian vehicles and parts would be "catastrophic for the entire industry," according to CNBC. The trigger is Jan. 1, the date President Trump set in August for doubling the current 25% rate if no deal emerges. The calendar, in other words, is the only party in these talks that has been perfectly clear about its position.

Thomas said she is "cautiously optimistic" that cooler heads will prevail. Translation: Honda has no way to influence the outcome and has decided that hope is a reasonable line item. Her optimism rests on recent reports that Washington and Ottawa have restarted talks, including on easing levies on critical materials such as aluminum.

What Honda really wants is not a deal but a bigger deal. Thomas said the company prefers a three-country arrangement including Mexico, like the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement, or USMCA, over separate bilateral arrangements. CNBC reported that trade groups for Honda and every major U.S. automaker have lobbied the same way. Translation: when the entire industry agrees on something, it is usually because the alternative involves a spreadsheet nobody wants to build.

The reason is parts. Many automotive officials have raised concerns because components cross North American borders repeatedly during vehicle production, so a tariff is not paid once but can be paid at several stops along the way. A bolt that goes to Canada and back does not experience this as a vacation.

The USMCA itself is in an awkward state. Trump negotiated it in his first term to replace NAFTA, and it took effect in 2020. He later soured on it and accused Canada of "ripping off the United States of America for years." U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer announced months ago that the U.S. would not automatically extend the pact, shifting it from a 16-year trilateral extension to an annual review. Translation: instead of a long lease, the deal is now month-to-month with an annual inspection.

Honda is the second-largest vehicle producer in Canada behind Toyota, but the company says more than 60% of the vehicles it sells in the U.S. are built domestically at multiple U.S. assembly plants. That is a meaningful cushion, though Thomas made clear it does not make the industry immune. She said she never thought she would see North America put at such a disadvantage, noting that some overseas countries have better tariff rates.

She has a point on the numbers. CNBC noted the Trump administration has struck deals with Japan and South Korea, both major vehicle exporters to the U.S., that include 15% tariffs on vehicles. Canadian vehicles face 25% now and possibly 50% in the new year, meaning a neighbor with an integrated supply chain could pay more than distant exporters.

Markets, for now, are not panicking. SPY closed at 769.14 on Oct. 27 and the VIX, Wall Street's fear gauge, stood at 18.39 on Oct. 26, a number that suggests investors are concerned but not yet rearranging their furniture. With about two months left, the question is whether negotiators move before the date does.
articles.wire_headline: Honda warns 50% Canada auto tariffs would be catastrophic for auto industry

articles.headline: JetBlue Stock Jumps 20% After Airline Promises Profit, Eventually, in Writing
articles.dek: Shares surged after JetBlue set a new profit target and argued its bond selloff doesn't match its earnings, according to MarketWatch and Investing.com.
articles.catch_up: JetBlue has lost money for years, and its bonds have been sold off hard enough to raise questions about whether it can keep operating. This week the airline published a profit target and said investors were misreading the situation.
articles.why_it_matters: When a heavily indebted airline's bonds fall, borrowing gets costlier and the risk of a restructuring rises, which can affect ticket prices, routes and jobs. A 20% stock rally on a promise shows how much of the airline's value rests on whether lenders believe it.
body: JetBlue's stock rose more than 20% after the airline laid out a new profit target, MarketWatch reported. The paper described the target as calming fears about the airline's viability. Translation: investors had been wondering whether the company would survive, and a spreadsheet with a positive number at the end was enough to cheer them up.

The backdrop, per MarketWatch, is that JetBlue has been losing money for years. Years of losses are normally a reason for investors to hold a tense meeting. A target is not a profit, but it is the first document in a while that contains the word, so the market took it as progress.

Investing.com reported a second part of the pitch: JetBlue flagged a 'disconnect' between its earnings and the rout in its bonds. Translation: the airline says lenders are pricing it as if disaster is near, while its operating results suggest a less dramatic picture. This is the corporate version of telling a landlord that the neighbors are exaggerating the fire.

The bond angle matters more than it sounds. Bonds are loans investors make to a company, and when their prices fall, the yield, or the interest rate the company would need to pay to borrow again, rises. With the 10-year Treasury at 5.0% and the 2-year at 4.69% as of October 23, the safe baseline is already high, so a risky borrower has to offer much more on top. An airline with big debts and a history of losses sits at the expensive end of that menu.

That is why the stock reacted so sharply. Shareholders sit behind lenders in line, so if the bond market doubts the company, stockholders get nervous first and loudest. A credible path to profit reassures both groups, at least until the next quarter's results show whether the path was a road or a drawing.

There is also an outside factor. Brent crude stood at 115.22 as of October 20, and fuel is among an airline's largest costs. Neither source in this case tied JetBlue's plan to oil prices, so readers should note only that the target will have to survive the fuel bill, whatever it turns out to be.

For ordinary travelers, the stakes are practical. A airline that is not in financial trouble keeps flying its routes and honoring its tickets, while one that is may cut service or raise fares to fix its books. A 20% jump in the shares suggests investors now think that outcome is less likely, though the bonds, which started this, will get the final say.
What to watch: whether the bond prices recover. Stock traders can be convinced by a target in a day, but lenders usually want to see the profit first.
articles.wire_headline: JetBlue has been losing money for years. It just charted a path to profitability.
